title: Nothing to hide?
summary_es: Ensayo argumentativo que desmonta, supuesto a supuesto, la idea de que «quien nada esconde, nada teme» ante la vigilancia.
prediction_prompt: "If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear." How convincing do you find this argument, and why?

sentences.text: Whenever a new form of surveillance is proposed, someone can be relied upon to observe that those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear.
The remark has the comforting ring of common sense, which is precisely why it deserves closer inspection.
It rests on at least three assumptions, none of which survives much scrutiny.
The first is that privacy is essentially about concealing wrongdoing.
Yet most of what we keep to ourselves is not shameful at all.
We close the bathroom door, seal our letters and lower our voices in restaurants, not because we are plotting anything, but because certain parts of life are simply not addressed to an audience.
Few of us would hand a stranger our diary, however dull its contents.
To ask what a person has to hide is therefore to ask the wrong question.
A better one would be why anybody else should be entitled to look.
The second assumption is that information, once collected, will only ever be used for the purpose originally announced.
History offers little encouragement here.
Records gathered for one reason have a habit of proving useful for another, and the people who decide what counts as suspicious are not always the people who made the original promise.
A list of those who attended a perfectly legal demonstration may seem harmless under one government and become considerably less so under the next.
Data, unlike political intentions, tends to last.
It would be reassuring to think that such abuses belong to the past, or to other countries, but there is little evidence that any nation is immune.
The third assumption, and arguably the most misleading, is that being watched leaves our behaviour unchanged.
Anyone who has tried to sing in front of strangers knows otherwise.
Studies of people who believe their searches are monitored suggest that they become more cautious about what they look up, avoiding topics that are entirely lawful but might be misinterpreted.
Nobody has forbidden them anything.
They have merely concluded that curiosity carries a risk, and adjusted accordingly.
A society in which large numbers of citizens quietly make that calculation is poorer for it, even if not a single person is ever arrested.
There is a further difficulty, which the phrase conveniently ignores.
It imagines surveillance as a matter of isolated facts, each of them innocent enough: a purchase here, a journey there, a telephone call lasting four minutes.
But modern systems do not examine facts in isolation.
They combine them, and the combination can reveal what no single item would.
A person's religion, state of health or financial troubles may never have been recorded anywhere, and yet be perfectly obvious to anyone holding a year of their movements and payments.
In such circumstances it is hardly reassuring to be told that one has nothing to hide, since one can no longer be sure what one is showing.
None of this amounts to an argument against all forms of monitoring.
There are, undeniably, crimes that cannot be investigated without access to private communications, and it would be naive to pretend that every objection to surveillance is made in good faith.
Those who defend privacy sometimes speak as though any intrusion whatsoever marked the first step towards tyranny, which does their cause few favours.
The serious question is not whether the state may ever look, but under what conditions, with whose permission and for how long.
What the "nothing to hide" argument does, in effect, is to shift the burden of proof.
Instead of requiring those who wish to watch to justify themselves, it invites those who would rather not be watched to explain what they are concealing.
Framed in that way, the debate is over before it has begun, since a preference for privacy is itself treated as grounds for suspicion.
It is a neat rhetorical trick, and an effective one.
It is worth remembering that the people who repeat the phrase most confidently tend to have curtains on their windows and passwords on their phones.
They are right to.
Privacy is not the refuge of the guilty; it is the ordinary condition of a life that belongs to the person living it.
The burden of explanation should rest, as it does in every other sphere, on whoever proposes to take something away.

language_focus.explanation_es: El ensayo rara vez afirma en seco: *arguably the most misleading* (se podría sostener que), *tends to last* (suele), *may seem harmless* (puede parecer), *it would be naive to pretend* (sería ingenuo). Estas fórmulas hacen el argumento más difícil de rebatir, porque no promete más de lo que puede demostrar.

El párrafo 6 reconoce lo que hay de cierto en la postura contraria (*None of this amounts to…*, *There are, undeniably…*) y critica a los propios aliados. Es una estrategia clásica del ensayo argumentativo: quien concede parece más fiable cuando después vuelve a atacar (párrafo 7).

tasks.prompt: What is the writer's overall position?

options.text: Governments should be forbidden from monitoring citizens under any circumstances
Privacy matters less now that most people share their lives online
A popular defence of monitoring depends on beliefs that do not hold
Only those who break the law need to worry about being observed

tasks.rationale_es: El ensayo examina los supuestos del «nada que esconder» y concluye que ninguno resiste. No pide prohibir toda vigilancia: el párrafo 6 lo descarta expresamente.

tasks.prompt: Match paragraphs 2, 3, 4 and 5 with the best heading. There is one extra heading.

headings.text: Promises do not outlive those who make them
The whole reveals more than its parts

tasks.rationale_es: P2 redefine la privacidad; p3 advierte de que los datos sobreviven a quien prometió usarlos bien; p4 muestra que vigilar cambia la conducta; p5 explica que combinar datos sueltos revela lo que ninguno revela por sí solo. Del coste de la tecnología no se habla.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer mention closing the bathroom door?

options.text: To show that wanting privacy is ordinary, not a sign of guilt
To suggest that private homes are the only places still free from observation
To argue that people are more secretive than they admit
To compare modern habits with those of earlier times

tasks.rationale_es: Los tres ejemplos son cosas que hacemos sin tramar nada: sirven para probar que casi todo lo que reservamos no es vergonzoso.

tasks.prompt: Which is closest in meaning to "scrutiny" in paragraph 1?

options.text: public support
close examination
legal challenge
repeated use over time

tasks.rationale_es: La frase anterior pide *closer inspection*; *scrutiny* recoge esa misma idea: los supuestos no aguantan que se los mire de cerca.

tasks.prompt: According to the writer, collected information usually disappears when a government changes.
tasks.rationale_es: Dice lo contrario: los datos, a diferencia de las intenciones políticas, *tend to last*, y una lista inofensiva con un gobierno puede dejar de serlo con el siguiente.

tasks.prompt: What point does the writer make with the example of monitored searches?

options.text: Monitoring makes illegal activity far less common
Most users have no idea that anyone is watching them
Search engines often misunderstand what users are asking
People limit themselves even when no rule requires it

tasks.rationale_es: Evitan temas totalmente legales y *nobody has forbidden them anything*: se autocensuran porque han concluido que la curiosidad tiene un riesgo.

options.text: Judging that being inquisitive is not worth the danger
Working out how many citizens the authorities have detained
Estimating how much monitoring costs the state
Deciding which topics are against the law

tasks.rationale_es: *That calculation* retoma la frase anterior: han concluido que la curiosidad entraña un riesgo y se han adaptado.

tasks.prompt: What is the function of paragraph 6 ("None of this amounts to…")?

options.text: To introduce the strongest objection to privacy and accept it in full
To summarise the three assumptions
To acknowledge the limits of the writer's own case
To describe how investigations are carried out

tasks.rationale_es: Es una concesión: admite que hay delitos que exigen acceso a comunicaciones privadas y que no toda objeción es de buena fe, antes de volver a su tesis.

tasks.prompt: How does the writer regard some defenders of privacy?

options.text: As dishonest about their real motives
As harming their case by overstating it
As the only voices that can be relied on in this debate
As too willing to compromise

tasks.rationale_es: Hablan como si cualquier intromisión fuera el primer paso hacia la tiranía, *which does their cause few favours*: exagerar les perjudica.

tasks.prompt: The writer thinks the state should never be allowed to read private communications.
tasks.rationale_es: La pregunta seria *is not whether the state may ever look*, sino en qué condiciones, con permiso de quién y durante cuánto tiempo.

tasks.prompt: The writer has personally been placed under surveillance.
tasks.rationale_es: El ensayo argumenta en general y no cuenta ninguna experiencia personal de vigilancia.

tasks.prompt: Why does the writer mention curtains and passwords in the final paragraph?

options.text: To suggest that technology has made homes less safe
To prove that most people are hiding something illegal
To recommend simple ways of protecting oneself from criminals
To show that the argument's supporters value privacy in practice

tasks.rationale_es: Quienes repiten la frase con más aplomo tampoco renuncian a su intimidad: su conducta contradice lo que dicen, y el autor añade que hacen bien.

tasks.prompt: Complete the summary with one word from paragraphs 7 and 8 in each gap.
tasks.text: The phrase shifts the {{1}} of proof onto those who want privacy, treating their preference as {{2}} for suspicion. For the writer, privacy is not the {{3}} of the guilty.
tasks.rationale_es: *shift the burden of proof* (trasladar la carga de la prueba), *grounds for suspicion* (motivo de sospecha) y *the refuge of the guilty* (el refugio de los culpables).
